briefing.text: Chromoplexy (chains of interdependent translocations and deletions) is inferred from junction-level structural-variant calls that give both breakpoint coordinates and orientations for each junction (the input ChainFinder-type methods need). Before any chain analysis, list the columns of data_sv.txt and check whether both sites have chromosome, position and strand fields, and count rows per sample. If those fields are missing, chains cannot be reconstructed from this table; say the chain-inference variable is absent rather than building an ad hoc proxy and calling it chromoplexy.
briefing.reason: Whether the data can test the central claim depends on this; it decides what analysis is even possible.

briefing.text: cBioPortal SV files often hold only curated fusions (e.g. ETS/ERG fusions), not the full somatic rearrangement catalogue. Compare the number of SV rows with the number of samples and tabulate Event_Info and genes. If the table is essentially a fusion annotation, a lack of chains or few rearrangements in it says nothing about whether rearrangements are rare or unchained.
briefing.reason: Stops the team reading an incomplete SV table as negative evidence.

briefing.text: Copy-number segments (data_cna_hg19.seg, data_cna, data_log2_cna) show where copy number changes, but not which breakpoint ends are joined to which partner. Deletion bridges and rearrangement chains cannot be rebuilt from segments alone. Check the seg file's columns. Any seg-based analysis, such as counting deletions on several chromosomes, is at best a weak proxy: report it as one, and do not treat co-occurring deletions as proof that they formed together.
briefing.reason: This is the most tempting substitute analysis, and it does not measure interdependence.

briefing.text: TMPRSS2-ERG fusion arises either through an interstitial deletion of about 3 Mb on 21q22 or through a balanced translocation or insertion. A chr21 deletion or an ERG fusion alone does not demonstrate chromoplexy. The hypothesis's second part, that chromoplexy dysregulates prostate cancer genes (e.g. ERG, PTEN, TP53, CHEK2, NKX3-1), needs data linking chain breakpoints to those genes. Tabulate ERG fusion status from the SV table and any clinical fusion columns (e.g. ERG_FISH_RESULT, ETS_FUSION_SEQ), and check whether anything ties these genes to multi-partner events.
briefing.reason: Single-gene fusion or deletion events are easy to mistake for evidence about the gene-dysregulation part.

briefing.text: Label logic: 'False' needs the relevant variables to be present and analysed, with results that contradict the claim. Missing junction or chain data means evidence is absent, not contrary. In the other direction, published reports of how common chromoplexy is in prostate cancer must not stand in for analysing these files. Before choosing a label, list which parts of the hypothesis (rearrangement chains, interdependent formation, dysregulation of cancer genes) have a matching variable in the data, and test the parts that do.
briefing.reason: Tells the team how to map what is present or missing in the data onto the three labels, without prior knowledge deciding the answer.

briefing.text: Low tumour purity and subclonality reduce sensitivity for deletions and low-copy junctions, and results from different assays (WGS vs exome or panel) are not comparable. Check the purity columns in the clinical tables and data_gene_panel_matrix.txt (the structural_variants column) to see which samples were actually profiled for SVs. Restrict to those samples, or stratify by assay and purity.
briefing.reason: Changes which samples go into any rearrangement or copy-number analysis.

briefing.text: Chromoplexy calls rest on arbitrary thresholds. For example, JaBbA requires at least 3 low-copy junctions (junction copy number <=3) with breakpoints within 10 kb, spanning more than 10 Mb across at least 3 separate genomic territories; ChainFinder requires closed chains with little copy change. If you attempt any chain or proxy call, state the exact definition you used and check how sensitive the result is to the thresholds.
briefing.reason: Any call the team makes needs a stated, sensitivity-checked definition.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed chromoplexy can only be tested by full chain reconstruction from junction-level SV calls with coordinates and strands, and that any weaker evidence is not relevant. Neither team checked whether the hypothesis's second clause (chromoplexy dysregulating prostate cancer genes) has partial variables in the data that could be examined.

Both treated data_sv.txt as the only rearrangement evidence and read its 28 fusion rows as a curated list. Neither checked whether the 57 WGS samples, all marked as SV-profiled in the gene panel matrix, have rearrangement information encoded somewhere else, such as clinical fusion-mechanism columns or seg breakpoints at fusion genes.
unused_evidence: ERG_FISH_RESULT separates 'Translocation' from 'Translocation with deletion', so it records the mechanism of fusion formation (deletion-linked versus balanced or insertional). Team A tabulated it but did not ask whether it bears on translocations and deletions arising together.

ETS_FUSION_SEQ names fusion partners and types (TMPRSS2-ERG, SLC45A3-ERG, NRF1-BRAF, intergenic ETV1). The interchromosomal partners (SLC45A3 on chr1 with ERG on chr21, NRF1 on chr7 with BRAF on chr7, ETV1 intergenic) are rearrangements that cross territories. Neither team used the partner chromosomes.

The seg file (58 samples) and the gene-level CNA matrices could show whether copy-number breakpoints sit at the fusion genes and at classic prostate cancer genes (e.g. deletions at PTEN, NKX3-1, CHD1 or TP53) in fusion-positive samples. Neither team looked at breakpoint positions relative to those genes.

The mutation table holds a few non-coding WGS rows (IGR, Intron, RNA). This suggests the SNV calls were filtered to near-coding regions, but it does not affect SV availability. One sample has no mutation profile in the panel matrix.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A named the risk that the study is the source of the claim and that a grader expects True. It did not resolve this with the data. It only said junction data are missing and did not check whether any column (FISH mechanism, fusion partner) gives partial support.

Team B named a deletion-at-fusion proxy as its weakest point and dismissed it without running it. It did not report how many fusion-positive samples show a 21q22 deletion between TMPRSS2 and ERG in the seg file, or whether that agrees with the FISH 'with deletion' calls.
second_readings: The hypothesis could be read as two claims. (a) A modelling method can identify interdependent translocations and deletions. (b) These events frequently dysregulate prostate cancer genes. Claim (b) could be partly checked: are rearrangements that join fusion and deletion events at cancer genes frequent in this cohort? Claim (a) needs junction data.

'Frequently' can be read as a cohort-level frequency (the share of tumours with such events). The fusion and FISH columns give a cohort-level frequency of fusion-mediated dysregulation of ETS genes even though chains are absent. Whether that frequency is relevant to the label depends on whether chromoplexy is taken to require proven chains.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust in 'Not verifiable'. Junction-level data needed to reconstruct chromoplexy chains really are absent. But both teams under-used the FISH fusion-mechanism column and the seg breakpoints at fusion and cancer genes, which bear partly on the 'dysregulation of prostate cancer genes' clause, so the absence of relevant variables has not been fully shown.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: ERG_FISH_RESULT separates 'Translocation' from 'Translocation with deletion'. Cross-tabulate it against ETS_FUSION_SEQ and against a 21q22 deletion between TMPRSS2 and ERG in data_cna_hg19.seg. Does this column count as a variable that records translocations and deletions arising together, and does that change your inventory of relevant variables or your label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: In fusion-positive and fusion-negative samples, tabulate copy-number breakpoints or deletions in data_cna.txt and the seg file at canonical prostate cancer genes (e.g. PTEN, NKX3-1, CHD1, TP53). Do deletions at these genes co-occur with the fusion events more than in fusion-negative samples? Is any such pattern relevant to the 'dysregulation of prostate cancer genes' clause, and does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your weakest point is the expectation that a grader will want True. List each clause of the hypothesis, the variable in the data that matches it (if any), and the result for that clause. Does any clause have a variable you have not yet analysed, and does that change your label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You named the TMPRSS2-ERG deletion proxy as your weakest point but did not run it. For every ERG-fusion-positive sample, check the seg file for a deletion between TMPRSS2 and ERG on chr21, and compare the result with ERG_FISH_RESULT ('Translocation' vs 'Translocation with deletion'). Does this check change which variables you count as relevant, or your label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your audit covered data_sv.txt and ETS_FUSION_SEQ. Did you also use the partner genes named in ETS_FUSION_SEQ (e.g. SLC45A3, NRF1, intergenic ETV1) to find rearrangements between chromosomes, and did you check the seg file for copy-number breakpoints at those partners? Does any of this give partial evidence about rearrangements across several territories, and does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: data_gene_panel_matrix.txt marks 57 samples as WGS-profiled for structural variants, but data_sv.txt has 28 rows. Compare the SV-table samples with the fusion-positive samples from the clinical columns, and check for fusion-positive samples missing from the SV table and the reverse. findings.question: In the original definition of chromoplexy in prostate cancer, what input data and criteria are needed to call a chromoplexy event? Can it be inferred from copy-number segments or from fusion-level annotations alone?
findings.answer: Baca et al. 2013 (Cell) called chromoplexy from whole-genome sequencing using ChainFinder. ChainFinder builds a graph with rearrangement breakpoints as nodes (junction-level SV calls, each with paired breakends) and chromosomal deletion segments ('deletion bridges' taken from copy-number data) as edges. It then searches for sets of connected breakpoints that are statistically unlikely to have arisen independently. The resulting chains run from 3 to more than 40 rearrangements, often across several chromosomes and often closed and near-balanced, with little copy-number change. Chromoplexy cannot be called from copy-number segments alone or from fusion annotations alone: breakpoint-resolved rearrangement junctions are required, and copy-number data only adds deletion bridges that link junctions together. A fusion call or a FISH result may suggest that a fusion is part of a chain, but it does not show it.

The resulting chains run from 3 to more than 40 rearrangements, often across several chromosomes and often closed and near-balanced, with little copy-number change. findings.question: How often does TMPRSS2-ERG fusion arise as part of a chromoplexy chain rather than a simple interstitial deletion, and can the two be told apart by FISH break-apart patterns ('translocation' vs 'translocation with deletion')?
findings.answer: In Baca et al. 2013, chromoplexy disrupted ERG through TMPRSS2-ERG in 15 of 26 fusion-positive tumours (about 58%). This figure comes from Garraway's NHGRI slides summarising the study, and the PMC commentary says the fusion was 'often found as part of chromoplectic rearrangement chains'. Berger et al. 2011 had already reported closed chains of balanced rearrangements in ETS-positive tumours. ERG break-apart FISH and three-colour FISH only sort fusions into two classes: translocation or insertion (split signal, 5-prime ERG kept) and deletion (5-prime ERG lost through interstitial 21q22 deletion). FISH cannot resolve breakpoints. A chromoplexy chain may also carry deletion bridges, so it could show either FISH pattern. I found no source that maps the FISH class onto chromoplexy status, so a FISH mechanism column is at best weak, indirect evidence and cannot identify interdependent rearrangements. I could not read the primary Baca full text that gives the 15/26 figure; the pages I could open were truncated.
